summary.text: Recombination is the era when free electrons and protons first bound together into electrically neutral hydrogen atoms.
It happened about 378,000 years after the Big Bang, once the universe had cooled enough that the radiation could no longer instantly knock atoms apart.
It is a distinct event from photon decoupling, which occurred in the same time frame and is the step that resulted in the cosmic microwave background radiation.

items.prompt: A student says recombination means electrons and protons were joined once, split apart, and then joined again. Is this right?

items.prompt: Just before recombination, energetically favoured atoms still could not last. What stopped them?

options.label: There were too few electrons to join protons
Hydrogen refused to bond at any temperature
The protons moved too fast to catch electrons

items.explain: Atoms could form energetically, but one of the vast number of photons would immediately ionize them, until the universe cooled enough.

items.prompt: Imagine two clocks, one marking atoms forming and one marking light starting to travel freely. They tick at nearly the same moment. Are they the same event?

Yes, they are two names for one process

items.explain: They occurred in the same time frame, but are distinct events based on different physical processes.

items.prompt: What lets the huge number of photons travel without scattering, so that they become the cosmic microwave background?

options.label: Expansion thins out the free electrons
Photons turn into matter as they cool
Helium absorbs them all
Electrons grow heavier and slow down

items.explain: Photon decoupling happened when expansion diluted the electrons, so the photons could propagate without scattering.

items.prompt: A fast shortcut for forming hydrogen would be an electron dropping straight to the lowest energy level. Why does this work poorly?

options.label: It needs far more electrons than exist
It releases a photon that almost immediately re-ionizes a nearby atom

items.explain: Each direct recombination to the ground state gives off a photon above 13.6 eV, which almost immediately re-ionizes a neighbouring hydrogen atom.

items.prompt: Today's microwave background is at 2.7 K, and the shift is given by T = 2.7 K × (1 + z). Roughly how did the temperature at z = 1100 compare with today's?

options.label: About the same temperature
About 1,100 times cooler

paragraphs.heading: When atoms first formed
paragraphs.text: In cosmology, recombination is the era when charged electrons and protons first locked together into hydrogen atoms with no overall electric charge. It took place roughly 378000 years after the Big Bang, when the redshift was z = 1100. Redshift, written z, measures how much the expansion of the universe has since shifted the energy of light.

paragraphs.heading: A misleading name
paragraphs.text: The "re-" in recombination is misleading. The Big Bang theory does not say that protons and electrons were ever joined before this. The name is a leftover from history, since it was coined before the Big Bang became the main theory of how the universe was born.

paragraphs.heading: Why atoms had to wait
paragraphs.text: Just before recombination, the universe held few neutral hydrogen atoms. In terms of energy, atoms could already form, but one of the enormous number of photons would ionize each one straight away, splitting it apart again. In time the universe cooled until the radiation could no longer do that at once, and atoms became the favoured state.

paragraphs.heading: Not the same as decoupling
paragraphs.text: Photon decoupling, when light began moving freely through the universe without interacting with matter, happened in the same period. Still, the two are separate events driven by different physics. Recombination came as expansion lowered the temperature, producing atoms and some photons. Decoupling came as expansion thinned out the electrons, so the far larger crowd of photons could travel without scattering, and that light became the cosmic microwave background.

paragraphs.heading: Dating it from the CMB
paragraphs.text: The timing can be estimated from how the temperature of the cosmic microwave background (CMB) changes over time. The CMB is a blackbody spectrum of the photons that existed at recombination, with their energy shifted by cosmic expansion. Its temperature follows T_CMB = 2.7 K × (1 + z), with today's value being 2.7 K. With the ratio of baryons, or ordinary matter, to photons near 10⁻⁹, a figure known partly from the Planck satellite, the sum gives z_rec around 1100, or about 400,000 years.

paragraphs.heading: Slower than a simple sum
paragraphs.text: A simple equilibrium calculation, asking when half the hydrogen is ionized, gives a recombination temperature of about 4000 K at redshift z = 1500. In 1968, Jim Peebles in the US and Yakov Zel'dovich and colleagues in the USSR each worked out the non-equilibrium history on their own. An electron dropping straight into hydrogen's ground state gets little done, because it gives off a photon above 13.6 eV that soon re-ionizes a neighbouring atom. So electrons join excited states instead and cascade quickly down to the first excited state, where n = 2. The resulting free electron fraction falls much more slowly than the equilibrium sum predicts, and the universe is 90% neutral at z ≈ 1070.

paragraphs.heading: Two ways down
paragraphs.text: From the first excited state, an atom has two routes to the ground state. From the 2p state it can emit a Lyman-α photon, but another ground-state hydrogen atom almost always soaks it up, unless cosmic redshifting moves it far enough off the line first. From the 2s state it can emit two photons, a slow process at 8.22 s⁻¹ that still competes with Lyman-α escape. Tracking hydrogen in its ground state, first excited state and ionized state is why this picture is called an effective three-level atom.
